# Diagnosing No-Crank, No-Start Conditions in Legacy GM Trucks

When a vehicle presents with a "no start/no crank" condition, but you have already validated the starter, battery, and starter relay, the diagnostic path shifts from simple component replacement to system-level signal tracing. In the specific case of a 2007 Silverado 1500 where interior functions like the radio and AC operate normally, yet the engine refuses to turn over when the key is turned further than the accessory position, the issue lies within the ignition switch's output circuit or the Powertrain Control Module (PCM) enable logic.

The symptom of a clicking relay while cranking suggests the starter solenoid is receiving an initial trigger pulse, but this does not guarantee the high-current load is being sustained long enough to engage the flywheel. More critically, the fact that bypassing the starter relay with a manual jumper wire allows the engine to crank successfully provides a definitive data point: the mechanical starter motor and its internal solenoid are functional. This isolates the fault to the electrical path between the ignition switch and the starter relay, or the ground return paths associated with that circuit.

In GM vehicles of this era, the ignition switch typically provides power to the starter relay coil in position 2 (Accessory/Run) and maintains that voltage while cranking. If the truck runs fine the day before and fails immediately after electrical work on unrelated systemsâsuch as repairing a trailer wiring harnessâit is highly probable that a ground strap was disturbed or a fuse connection loosened during the disassembly. Even if no visible damage exists, high-current circuits are sensitive to corrosion or poor contact points introduced by vibration or mechanical stress.

The diagnostic strategy here requires moving beyond visual inspection to voltage drop testing and circuit continuity checks. Start by verifying the power feed to the starter relay coil with a multimeter while an assistant turns the key to the "Start" position. You should see battery voltage at the coil supply terminal. If voltage is present but the relay does not click, the ground side of the relay coil circuit must be investigated. This often involves tracing the wire back to its termination point at the PCM or chassis ground.

Furthermore, consider the possibility of a blown fuse that was missed during the initial fuse box inspection. The source material mentions repairing a trailer turn signal circuit; in many GM trucks, the main battery fuse or the starter relay fuse is located in the same cluster. It is possible that excessive current drawn during the repair process caused a thermal fuse to blow, or that the act of removing and reinstalling the fuse box cover damaged a fuse tab. Before assuming a complex electronic failure within the PCM, ensure all fuses rated for the starter circuit (often 40A or higher) are intact and seated correctly.

If voltage is present at the relay coil and the fuse is good, but the starter still fails to engage via the ignition switch, you may be dealing with a failed ignition switch contact that only closes momentarily or loses ground control during cranking. In these scenarios, replacing the entire ignition switch assembly is often more cost-effective than repairing internal contacts. Always verify the battery state of charge under load; a battery that appears good at rest can collapse under the high amperage demand of the starter if it is aged or cold, leading to voltage drop issues that mimic electrical failures.

Finally, do not overlook the possibility of an open circuit in the wire between the ignition switch and the relay. Use a test light or multimeter to trace the path from the battery positive terminal, through the main fuse, to the relay coil input. If there is no continuity or significant resistance, you have identified the break. This approach ensures you address the root cause rather than swapping out components based on symptoms alone.
